'''The [[1986 in association football|1986]]–[[1987 in association football|87]] season''' was the 88th completed season of [[The Football League]].

Play-offs to determine promotion places were introduced in 1987 so that more clubs remained eligible for promotion closer to the end of the season, and at the same time to aid in the reduction over two years of the number of clubs in the First Division from 22 to 20.

At the same time, automatic promotion and relegation between the Fourth Division and the [[Football Conference]] was introduced for one club, replacing the annual application for [[Re-election (Football League)|re-election]] to the League of the bottom four clubs and linking the League to the developing [[National League System]] pyramid.

==Final league tables and results==
The tables and results below are reproduced here in the exact form that they can be found at [https://www.rsssf.org/engpaul/FLA/1986-87.html The Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation] website.<ref name="rsssf">{{cite web |url=https://www.rsssf.org/engpaul/FLA/1986-87.html |title=England 1986–87 |access-date=2010-02-24| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100127102628/http://www.rsssf.com/engpaul/FLA/1986-87.html| archive-date= 27 January 2010|website=[[RSSSF]]  <!--DASHBot-->| url-status= live}}</ref>

As of this season, there were no more re-election procedures, but instead, the club finishing last in the [[Football League Fourth Division|Fourth Division]] was demoted to [[Football Conference|Conference]]. The first casualty of this new practice were [[Lincoln City F.C.|Lincoln City]].

The First Division championship went to [[Everton F.C.|Everton]] in their final season under the management of [[Howard Kendall]] before his departure to [[Athletic Bilbao]]. This remains Everton's last league title. His side overcame a spate of injuries to fight off competition from runners-up [[Liverpool F.C.|Liverpool]] and third-placed [[Tottenham Hotspur F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]]. Fourth place went to George Graham's emerging young [[Arsenal F.C.|Arsenal]] side who also won the League Cup in his first season in charge. Fifth place went to newly-promoted [[Norwich City F.C.|Norwich City]], whose manager [[Ken Brown (footballer)|Ken Brown]] built a strong squad on a limited budget to achieve a finish which would have been enough to qualify for the [[UEFA Cup]] had it not been for the ongoing ban on English clubs in European competitions.

[[Wimbledon F.C.|Wimbledon]] finished sixth in the First Division in only their tenth season as a Football League club. [[Dave Bassett]]'s men had led the league for the first two weeks of September, but sixth place was still much higher than most pundits{{who|date=August 2023}} had predicted at the start of the season. [[Luton Town F.C.|Luton Town]] enjoyed their highest league position by finishing seventh.

[[Manchester United F.C.|Manchester United]] manager [[Ron Atkinson]] had been under pressure for months, after his side had finished fourth in the league in 1985–86, 12 points behind the champions, Liverpool. The Manchester United board had initially decided to stick with Atkinson as manager for the 1986–87 season, but finally sacked him in November with Manchester United fourth from bottom in the league and having suffered a League Cup exit to [[Southampton F.C.|Southampton]]. [[Aberdeen F.C.|Aberdeen]] manager [[Alex Ferguson]] took over, and results began to improve despite no immediate new signings being made, with Manchester United finally finishing 11th.

[[West Ham United F.C.|West Ham United]], who had come close to winning the title the previous season, slipped to 15th place in 1986–87.

[[Aston Villa F.C.|Aston Villa]] were relegated to the Second Division just five years after they won the European Cup. Chairman [[Doug Ellis]] had sensed from the start that 1986-87 would be a tough season for the club, so he axed manager [[Graham Turner]] in September and replaced him with [[Manchester City F.C.|Manchester City]]'s [[Billy McNeill]]. But McNeill was unable to stop the rot and Villa went down in bottom place. McNeill was subsequently sacked and replaced by Watford's [[Graham Taylor (football manager)|Graham Taylor]].

Villa were joined on the way down by [[Manchester City F.C.|Manchester City]] and [[Leicester City F.C.|Leicester City]]. In the first season of the relegation/promotion play-offs, [[Charlton Athletic F.C.|Charlton Athletic]] beat Second Division [[Leeds United F.C.|Leeds United]] to retain their top flight status.

No European qualification took place due to [[UEFA]] voting to ban English clubs from European competitions for a third season following the [[Heysel disaster]] in 1985.

==Second Division==
{{Infobox football league season
| competition        = [[Football League Second Division|Second Division]]
| season             = 1986–87
| winners            = [[Derby County F.C.|Derby County]]
| promoted           = [[Derby County F.C.|Derby County]]<br />[[Portsmouth F.C.|Portsmouth]]
| relegated          = [[Sunderland A.F.C.|Sunderland]]<br />[[Grimsby Town F.C.|Grimsby Town]]<br />[[Brighton & Hove Albion F.C.|Brighton & Hove Albion]]
| league topscorer   = [[Micky Quinn]]<br />(22 goals)<ref name="topscorers"/>

There were just two guaranteed promotion places in the Second Division this season due to the introduction of the playoffs and the phased reorganization of the league. [[Derby County F.C.|Derby County]] finished top of the Second Division to clinch a second successive promotion and reclaim the First Division place they had last held in 1980. [[Portsmouth F.C.|Portsmouth]], absent from the First Division for nearly 30 years and who had missed promotion by a single place in the previous two seasons, finally achieved promotion by finishing second. [[Oldham Athletic A.F.C.|Oldham Athletic]] and [[Ipswich Town F.C.|Ipswich Town]] failed to progress beyond the semi-finals of the new playoffs, leaving [[Leeds United F.C.|Leeds United]] to take on [[Charlton Athletic F.C.|Charlton Athletic]] in a two-legged contest for a First Division place. Charlton won the replay to keep their First Division status and condemn Leeds to a sixth successive season in the Second Division.

Financially troubled [[Grimsby Town F.C.|Grimsby Town]] were relegated, along with [[Brighton & Hove Albion]]. [[Sunderland A.F.C.|Sunderland's]] second relegation in three seasons condemned them to Third Division football for the first time in their history as they went down after losing in the playoffs.

==[[Football League Third Division|Third Division]]==
The three promotion places in this division were gained by three clubs who were among the least fancied promotion contenders at the start of the season. Champions [[AFC Bournemouth|Bournemouth]] were promoted to the Second Division for the first time in their history thanks to the efforts of hard working manager [[Harry Redknapp]]. Runners-up spot went to [[Bruce Rioch]]'s [[Middlesbrough F.C.|Middlesbrough]], who had begun the season on the verge of extinction and had been forced to play their first home game of the season at [[Hartlepool United F.C.|Hartlepool]]'s ground because the official receiver had locked them out of [[Ayresome Park]].

The relegation/promotion play-offs between the Third and Fourth Divisions saw [[Bolton Wanderers F.C.|Bolton Wanderers]] go down to the bottom division for the first time. [[Newport County A.F.C.|Newport County]], [[Darlington F.C.|Darlington]] and [[Carlisle United F.C.|Carlisle United]] went down automatically. The Fourth Division would be familiar territory for Newport and Darlington, but Carlisle had not played in the Fourth Division for nearly a quarter of a century and just three years earlier had been in the race for a First Division place. Defeat in the playoffs meant that [[Bolton Wanderers F.C.|Bolton Wanderers]] would be playing Fourth Division football for the first time in their history.

==[[Football League Fourth Division|Fourth Division]]==
The stars of the Fourth Division during 1986-87 were [[Graham Carr]]'s runaway champions [[Northampton Town F.C.|Northampton Town]], with young midfielder [[Eddie McGoldrick]] being the key player in his side's season of success. Northampton were confirmed as promoted with nine matches (19.6% of all matches) remaining, the earliest promotion in Football League history to date.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/article/2024/may/29/points-tallies-leverkusen-chelsea-knowledge|website=The Guardian|title=The Knowledge: Is Bayer Leverkusen's 40-point increase between seasons a record?|date=29 May 2024|accessdate=31 May 2024}}</ref>

Also automatically promoted were [[Preston North End F.C.|Preston North End]] and [[Southend United F.C.|Southend United]]. The fourth promotion place went to [[Aldershot F.C.|Aldershot]] by winning the promotion/relegation playoffs.

Down at the bottom end of the division, an injury time winner for [[Torquay United F.C.|Torquay United]] kept them in the Football League after a police dog had bitten one of their players. The introduction of automatic relegation to the Conference saw [[Lincoln City F.C.|Lincoln City]] lose their league status in favour of [[Football Conference|Conference]] champions [[Scarborough F.C.|Scarborough]].

[[Burnley F.C.|Burnley]] – league champions 27 years earlier – plummeted to new depths. They finished third from bottom in the league and only a win on the last day of the season prevented them from going down to the Conference.
